title: Breaker of the cruel
hookLine: khal khanddan hain, mahi manddan hain: He breaks the cruel and adorns the earth (Jaap, harbolmana)

cards: Anyone who has kept a garden knows the two jobs. One is planting: seeds, bulbs, the hopeful part. The other is pulling.
Bindweed wrapping around the beans. A vine strangling the rosebush. Pull them, and the garden breathes again; skip it, and no amount of planting will save it.
A good gardener is gentle and ruthless at once, and nobody calls that a contradiction. It's what loving a garden looks like. Jaap Sahib puts both jobs into a single rhyme.

teach.b: Right after karunaalay, the home of compassion, the harbolmana lines go on: khal khanddan hain, mahi manddan hain. Khal is the cruel one, the wicked, the person who preys on others; Punjabi still uses it for a scoundrel.
Mahi is the earth, and manddan is adorning, making beautiful. The two halves rhyme, khanddan, manddan, and the rhyme is the teaching. Breaking the cruel and adorning the earth aren't two jobs.

teach.h: ONE JOB, LIKE WEEDING A GARDEN.
teach.b: They're one, like pulling the bindweed so the roses can bloom.
And the line sits directly after compassion; Jaap doesn't separate them. In the Tenth Guru's world, compassion that never stood up to cruelty would be a kitchen with the door open to thieves.
The ideal of the saint-soldier, gentle in the heart and ready in the hands, is in these tiny lines. The breaking is never the point on its own.
Cruelty gets broken so that the earth can be adorned: fed, sheltered, made fair. And the week ends here. Six days ago, Jaap switched into Persian and called the One the lamp of beauty.
Then the provider, giver of daily bread. Gobind, generous and infinite. One form, seen in countless ways.
The ender and sustainer of all. The house of compassion. And today, the breaker of the cruel, who adorns the earth.

how: Sikhs recite the harbolmana lines, karunaalay hain, khal khanddan hain, mahi manddan hain, briskly each morning in Jaap Sahib, and the saint-soldier ideal joins compassion with standing up to cruelty.

o: a sword that cuts in two directions
punishing every person who does wrong
breaking the cruel so the earth can flourish

games.q: breaker of the cruel — tap the pairs.

s: this line comes right after the home of compassion
karunaalay hain, then khal khanddan hain: Jaap keeps them together.
in Jaap, breaking cruelty is the goal in itself
the goal is mahi manddan, a more beautiful earth.
khanddan and manddan rhyme on purpose
breaking the cruel and adorning the earth are one job.

games.q: you're a gardener who loves your roses. bindweed is strangling them. what does loving the garden look like?
o: pull the weed so the roses can bloom.
plant more roses and ignore the weed.
games.why: khal khanddan, mahi manddan: breaking what's cruel and adorning the earth are one act of care.

practice: Think about the day ahead and where a little cruelty might show up: a joke at someone's expense, gossip, a sharp tone with someone who can't answer back, your own inner voice being harsh with you.
Picture yourself not joining in, or gently changing the subject, and then picture one thing you could make a little more beautiful instead. Breathe.

wordCard.voice: Khal khanddan. The cruel one, broken — paired with mahi manddan, the earth adorned: the One who shatters cruelty and beautifies the world, in a single rhyme.

carryVoice: Your line: break cruelty, adorn earth. Planting and pulling are one job. Day three hundred fifty: a week, done.

sources.ref: Jaap Sahib, harbolmana chhand: karunaalay hain, ari ghaalay hain, khal khanddan hain, mahi manddan hain
